children: The Japanese semiconductor equipment maker will establish the centre in partnership with the Japanese government to train future fab and equipment engineers as India builds out its chip manufacturing ecosystem

Japanese semiconductor equipment maker Tokyo Electron (TEL) will establish a semiconductor training centre in Gujarat next year, as the company looks to build a specialised talent pipeline for India’s expanding chip manufacturing industry.

The centre will be established in partnership with the Japanese government and will focus on developing future fab engineers and semiconductor equipment engineers, Tokyo Electron president and CEO Toshiki Kawai said at Semicon India 2026 in New Delhi on Thursday.
“Developing semiconductor talent, including future fab engineers and equipment engineers, is critically important for the sustainable growth of the industry in India,” Kawai said.

The move comes as India builds out semiconductor manufacturing capacity, creating demand for engineers with expertise in semiconductor fabrication processes, equipment operation, maintenance and process control. Unlike conventional engineering roles, semiconductor manufacturing requires highly specialised knowledge of equipment and tightly controlled production environments.
For Tokyo Electron, which supplies equipment used in semiconductor production, building that skills base is also important to supporting its own long-term operations in India.

Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) has already selected TEL for a project to establish an HR development ecosystem for semiconductor manufacturing in India. Under the project, the company plans to create an HR development and service hub and work with local businesses and educational institutions to develop a self-sustaining programme for high-tech engineers.

Kawai said Tokyo Electron wanted to contribute to India's semiconductor industry by using its global expertise, while identifying talent development as a critical requirement for the industry's sustainable growth.

Kawai said the training centre would be established next year in partnership with the Japanese government. “India's semiconductor ecosystem is growing,” Kawai noted, attributing the expansion to government support and efforts by private companies.

The training centre adds a human-capital layer to India’s expanding semiconductor infrastructure. As new facilities come up, the availability of engineers capable of operating, maintaining and developing the technology used inside them will be critical to the pace at which the ecosystem can scale.
